findings.issue_text: [BUG] Create's error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) with the storage duration startStorage, recording a failed legacy write that never happened and losing the storage-failure metric. Dual-write dashboards show legacy create failures when unified storage create fails; the actual failed storage call is never counted, so migration monitoring under-reports storage errors and operators misdiagnose which backend is failing.

[BUG] Delete's success path calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...) passing the object name instead of options.Kind, and the error path also uses recordStorageDuration after declaring the metric kind from options.Kind. Prometheus label cardinality explodes: every deleted object's name becomes a metric label, unbounded cardinality in the dual-writer histogram/gauge, plus inconsistent labels between paths break aggregation.

[BUG] Delete reassigns ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the locally-built log variable, dropping the name/kind/method values it just attached, while log still logs with them. Any logger pulled from ctx inside legacy/storage Delete implementations sees the bare DualWriterMode3 logger without name/kind, so request-scoped log lines from downstream storage are uncorrelatable; whoever greps logs by object name during a delete incident gets nothing.

[BUG] Update's error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) using startStorage, so a failed unified-storage update is recorded as a failed legacy write and no storage metric is emitted. Same misattribution as Create: migration dashboards report legacy update failures that never occurred while real storage update errors vanish, blocking mode-3 health assessment during dual-write rollout.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's async legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy deletecollection latency/failures are recorded under the 'storage' metric. Legacy DeleteCollection outages are invisible in their own metric and pollute the storage metric; operators rolling out mode 3 cannot detect that legacy cleanup is timing out (10s timeout errors), so legacy rows silently accumulate.

[BUG] The async legacy Create goroutine derives its 10s-timeout context from the incoming request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...), but the parent request context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns, so the legacy write races request cancellation and can fail with 'context canceled' before the 10s timeout ever applies. Under any real HTTP client that cancels or under request-scoped context teardown, the legacy create is aborted, leaving unified storage and legacy storage permanently inconsistent — the exact split-brain mode 3 exists to prevent. The 10s timeout is dead code when the parent ctx dies first.

[BUG] The goroutine re-creates the object in legacy storage by calling d.Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer that Storage.Create already mutated (resourceVersion set), and the goroutine's error is only swallowed into a metric. Legacy create of an object already stamped with a unified-store resourceVersion fails or writes divergent metadata, and no log line, event, or retry records the loss — every failed legacy write in mode 3 is silent beyond a counter.

[BUG] Update's async legacy write passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is re-invoked against the legacy store's old object, producing a different object than what was written to unified storage. Legacy and unified stores diverge whenever the update function depends on the old object (e.g. resourceVersion-conflict checks or merge on old state): the same logical update writes different content to each backend, corrupting the migration source of truth.

[BUG] Update reads options.Kind for the log/metrics, but on the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration before any storage success, and there is no Get of the old object anymore, so an update that is a create (forceAllowCreate) in storage is never mirrored deterministically in legacy. Objects created via update-on-missing-name exist in unified storage but the legacy mirror depends on a racy goroutine with a possibly-cancelled context; rollback to mode 0 loses those objects.

[ADVISORY] List logs options.Kind and options.ResourceVersion, but recordStorageDuration is called with options.Kind while the other read path (Get) uses the same pattern with different option types — the label set now differs per method in ways only a lookup at the metric definition can confirm. Whoever builds dashboards across methods must handle per-method label inconsistencies; next change to dual-writer metrics requires touching five hand-maintained call sites with three different recorder names, which already drifted four times in this diff.

[ADVISORY] TestMode3_Create calls NewDualWriter(Mode3, ls, us, p) but never declares p in this test function, while TestMode3_Get declares p := prometheus.NewRegistry() locally — Create, List, Delete, DeleteCollection, and Update tests rely on a package-level p that this diff does not show being added. If no package-level p exists in pkg/apiserver/rest, the new mode 3 tests fail to compile, breaking CI for the whole package; the inconsistency between test functions also means each test registers metrics against different registries, so Create-path metrics go to a shared registry reused across tests, causing duplicate-metric panics on the second registration.

[ADVISORY] The diff deletes the local p := prometheus.NewRegistry() from TestMode1_Get but the file still references p in NewDualWriter, so the test now depends on a package-level p variable this diff does not add. Same compile failure risk: if p is not defined at package scope in this PR's other files, pkg/apiserver/rest tests do not build and the entire dual-writer test suite is blocked.

[ADVISORY] TestMode3_Create's success path asserts acc.GetResourceVersion() == "1" on exampleObj, which is a fixture whose resource version is defined outside this diff; the async legacy goroutine is never synchronized, so the legacy mock expectation m.On("Create", ...).Return(exampleObj, nil) is asserted by testify's mock assertion only if it runs. Flaky test: the goroutine's mock call may execute after the test function returns, producing intermittent 'mock: I don't know what to return' panics or missing-call assertion failures unrelated to the code under test; whoever touches mode 3 next inherits a flake.

[ADVISORY] The new 'dual write (etcd, mode 3)' subtest is immediately skipped via t.Skip("local etcd testing"), so the mode-3 etcd path has no automated coverage and the deletion-cleanup code below the skip is dead until someone unskips it. The etcd mode-3 path is untested CI-wise, and the DeleteCollection cleanup block after t.Skip never executes — a future unskip runs it against a possibly-unstarted etcd, failing confusingly.

[BUG] Create's storage-failure path calls recordLegacyDuration for a storage error, so storage failures are recorded as legacy-storage outcomes in the duration metrics. Dashboards monitoring dualwriter duration metrics by store see legacy-write latency/error histograms polluted by storage failures; storage failure rates appear near zero, misleading mode-3 migration health checks.

[BUG] Update's storage-failure path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, misattributing storage update failures to legacy. Metric consumers see legacy update failures that never happened and miss real storage update failures; alerting on storage health in mode 3 is broken.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration for the legacy DeleteCollection call. Legacy delete-collection latency is recorded under the storage label, so legacy performance and error rates are invisible and storage metrics are double-counted.

[BUG] Delete's success path passes `name` as the `kind` label to recordStorageDuration (options.Kind on the error path, name on the success path), producing inconsistent metric labels for the same series. The `kind` label splits into per-object-name values on success, exploding metric cardinality for delete-heavy resources and breaking kind-based aggregation.

[BUG] Delete sets `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of the enriched `log` it just built, so the timeout-cause context and legacy goroutine run without the kind/method/name logger values. Log lines emitted inside the legacy delete goroutine (e.g. via the timeout cause) lack kind, method, and name, making mode-3 delete troubleshooting unreliable.

[BUG] Update's async legacy call passes the raw `objInfo` instead of the previous `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`, so legacy re-computes the update against legacy's own old object rather than replaying the object unified storage produced. When legacy and unified objects have diverged (the exact situation dual-writing exists to converge), the legacy write computes a different updated object than storage, silently re-diverging the stores — the mode-3 convergence guarantee is dropped with no error or log.

[BUG] All four legacy writes (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) are fire-and-forget goroutines whose errors are never logged or surfaced, only folded into a duration metric — the previous synchronous per-method 'unable to create object in legacy storage' logging and any operator-visible signal of dual-write failure is removed. During migration mode 3, a broken legacy store fails silently: reads still work (from storage), but when the operator eventually promotes legacy or rolls back, data is missing with no log line or error explaining when the divergence began.

[BUG] TestMode3_Create's first case sets up a legacy Create mock but the test never asserts legacy was called (no Counts/Called assertion) and returns before the goroutine is guaranteed to run; Delete, DeleteCollection, and Update tests omit legacy mocks entirely so the async goroutine hits an unstubbed testify mock. An unstubbed testify mock method call panics inside the goroutine, so TestMode3_Delete/TestMode3_Update/TestMode3_DeleteCollection crash or pass nondeterministically (goroutine races the test's completion), and a regression that drops legacy writes entirely — mode 3's defining contract — passes the entire suite.

[BUG] TestMode3_Update's happy-path case mocks legacy Update with `mock.Anything` for objInfo and the test never inspects the object legacy received, so the updateWrapper removal (legacy now gets raw objInfo, not the storage-produced object) is completely uncovered. The legacy-gets-a-different-object-than-storage regression in this diff has no verification anywhere; doPlaylistTests in the integration test also reads only from unified storage, so nothing in the PR verifies the legacy write payload at all.

[ADVISORY] The new mode-3 integration subtests ('with dual write (file, mode 3)' and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)') reuse doPlaylistTests, which validates behavior through the API reading from unified storage, so no test in the diff verifies that legacy storage actually received the async writes (including after the 10s timeout boundary). Operators relying on mode 3 to keep legacy in sync for rollback have no acceptance criterion proving eventual legacy write success, timeout behavior, or ordering; a regression that never writes legacy passes all playlist mode-3 tests.

[ADVISORY] Create's async legacy goroutine shares the request's ctx-derived logger but is spawned from the request path with no bound on concurrent goroutines per request, and its 10s timeout cause is only observable if legacy reads the cause — there is no test of the timeout path anywhere in the diff. A slow legacy store turns every API create/update/delete into an extra 10s-lived goroutine with no backpressure; the timeout behavior (does legacy respect context cancellation mid-write, leaving a half-applied legacy write?) is untested and unverified.

[BUG] Create launches the legacy write in a goroutine that inherits the request-scoped ctx, so the legacy write is canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns and the parent context is canceled. The 10s WithTimeout does not detach from the request context; for any request whose response completes before the legacy write finishes (the normal case), ctx is canceled and the legacy store write fails with context.Canceled — Mode3's documented invariant 'writes to LegacyStorage and Storage' is silently violated and legacy storage ends up missing objects. Same pattern in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection goroutines.

[BUG] On storage Create failure the code records the failure via recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, attributing storage errors to the legacy metric. The unified-storage failure rate is underreported and the legacy metric shows phantom failures; anyone alerting on legacy-write health sees errors that never touched legacy storage.

[BUG] On storage Update failure the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) with the storage start time, mislabeling the storage error as a legacy error. Update failures in unified storage are recorded as legacy-write failures, corrupting both metric series for anyone migrating mode 3.

[BUG] The Update goroutine creates a context with WithTimeoutCause but the cancel is deferred with no path that ensures cancel runs before returning — and more concretely, the legacy write error is never logged, only turned into a metric. Operators lose the only synchronous signal that a legacy write diverged; a failed legacy update in mode 3 (the mode whose purpose is keeping legacy in sync until cutover) leaves legacy data silently stale with no log line to debug.

[BUG] The DeleteCollection goroutine records the legacy call's outcome with d.recordStorageDuration, so legacy delete-collection results are counted as storage metrics. Storage metrics show inflated counts and legacy DeleteCollection failures are invisible in the legacy series; the same mislabeling appears in the Create goroutine via recordLegacyDuration on a storage error (line ~37).

[BUG] On successful storage Delete, the duration is recorded with `name` (the object name) where every other call site passes `options.Kind`, producing an unbounded, per-object set of metric label values. Prometheus cardinality explodes: every deleted object name becomes a distinct label value, degrading the metrics backend and making per-kind dashboards wrong for delete.

[BUG] Delete no longer tolerates legacy NotFound: the old code explicitly skipped apierrors.IsNotFound from the legacy store, but the new async path records any legacy error (including NotFound during migration) as a failure with no filtering. During migration, objects that exist in storage but not in legacy will generate continuous legacy-delete failure metrics, and conversely the removal of the storage NotFound early-return check changes error propagation semantics from the reviewed mode-3 contract.

[BUG] TestMode3_Create references `p` in `NewDualWriter(Mode3, ls, us, p)` without declaring a local registry, unlike TestMode3_Get which declares `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()`. Unless a package-level `p` exists (a fragile, unclear test fixture), this file does not compile; even if it does resolve to a shared package-level registry, the Create test registers dual-writer collectors into a shared registry shared with other tests, causing duplicate-collector panics or cross-test interference.

[ADVISORY] The removal of `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` leaves NewDualWriter(Mode1, ls, us, p) depending on a package-level `p`, silently coupling the mode-1 test to a variable defined in another test file. The next contributor who removes or renames that fixture breaks this test file in a way the compiler message points at mode1_test.go, not the actual definition; test isolation also degrades since the registry is shared across all mode tests.

[ADVISORY] The happy-path Create test asserts acc.GetResourceVersion() == "1" and NotEqual(obj, anotherObj) without any test asserting that the legacy Create is actually invoked or that its failure is handled — the core invariant of mode 3 (dual write to legacy) has zero coverage in this rewritten suite. A regression that drops the legacy write entirely (e.g., a panic in the goroutine, or the ctx-cancellation bug) passes this suite; the old commented-out test at least asserted lsSpy.Counts("LegacyStorage.Create") == 1, and the rewrite deleted that coverage while claiming to add tests.

[ADVISORY] Update now delegates to d.Storage.Update with the raw objInfo instead of the previous get-then-wrap pattern (updateWrapper), so the legacy Update in the goroutine re-invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject — calling the user-supplied update function twice, concurrently, on different stores. Any UpdatedObject implementation with side effects (e.g., server-side apply, admission mutation, non-idempotent transforms like incrementing a counter) executes twice per update, and the object written to legacy can differ from the object written to storage — precisely the drift dual-write mode 3 exists to prevent.

[BUG] Mode 3's legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines spawned from the request context, so they routinely fail or are lost with no retry, queue, or reconciliation. The apiserver cancels the request context when the handler returns; the goroutine then calls d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete with an already-cancelled parent context (the 10s timeout child of a dead parent), so legacy writes fail immediately — and even when the process outlives the goroutine, a restart drops in-flight legacy writes. Legacy storage silently diverges from Unified Storage, so a later rollback or a mode-3 read of legacy-side data (dashboards folder trees, search) returns missing or stale objects with no error anywhere.

[BUG] On Storage.Create failure the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of d.recordStorageDuration, recording a legacy-write failure for a call that never touched legacy storage. Create-failure dashboards show a phantom legacy failure and a zero storage failure; operators debugging dual-write health are actively misled on the exact path (unified-store create failure) they most need to see.

[BUG] On Storage.Update failure the code records d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), misattributing a unified-store failure to legacy using the storage start time. Update-failure metrics attribute storage errors to legacy, corrupting both the error-rate and duration series operators use to decide when it is safe to migrate modes; the storage failure counter stays zero while legacy's shows phantom failures.

[BUG] The DeleteCollection goroutine records the legacy call's outcome with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency and failures are logged as storage metrics. DeleteCollection is the one bulk path that can miss many legacy rows at once; its failures are hidden entirely from the legacy metrics series, and the storage series is polluted, so a diverging legacy store looks healthy on every dashboard.

[BUG] Delete builds a log with name/kind/method via WithValues but then calls ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), binding the base logger instead of the enriched one. Every log line emitted inside the legacy delete goroutine and the delete error paths carries neither the name, kind, nor method field, making delete failures unattributable in a multi-kind dual-write deployment where this logger was introduced specifically to add that context.

[BUG] On successful Storage.Delete the metric label is recorded as d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) — passing the object's name where every other call site passes options.Kind. The kind label of the storage-delete duration histogram becomes the deleted object's name, so per-kind delete dashboards fragment into unbounded label values (one series per name) and the true kind is never recorded; downstream aggregation on kind silently drops these samples.

[ADVISORY] The Update goroutine passes the caller's rest.UpdatedObjectInfo to Legacy.Update concurrently with having already used it for Storage.Update, so legacy derives its own updated object from legacy state instead of receiving the object unified storage wrote. The previous code wrapped objInfo in updateWrapper specifically to force legacy to store the identical object unified storage stored; removing that wrapper lets legacy apply objInfo against a different old object, so the two stores can hold different content for the same resource (and objInfo implementations that read the request body or are not safe for a second, concurrent, delayed invocation will error or double-apply). Counter-argument — the timeout bounds it and objInfo is usually pure — fails because objInfo is an arbitrary caller-supplied closure the dual writer cannot assume is idempotent or thread-safe.

[ADVISORY] Every write request now unconditionally spawns an unbounded goroutine holding the request's obj/options with no queue, worker pool, or backpressure, and the 10-second timeout literal is duplicated as a bare time.Second*10 across four sites. A write burst spawns one goroutine per request against a legacy store with a fixed connection pool; goroutines pile up behind it for 10s each, multiplying memory pressure during the exact bursts where the request path is already saturated, and any per-store latency spike converts into O(requests) queued goroutines. The four copies of time.Second*10 (and the four 'legacy X timeout' error strings) will drift independently on the next edit of one path. Counter-argument — 10s is generous — fails because the guard is per-request, not system-wide, so it bounds nothing under load.

[ADVISORY] Create/Update/List read options.Kind as the metric/log discriminator, but DeleteOptions and UpdateOptions in k8s API calls are routinely sent without Kind populated, so the kind label is an empty string for real client traffic. Per-kind dual-write dashboards silently show zero activity for the most common paths (kubectl/SDK clients don't set Kind on options) while the integration tests — which construct options with TypeMeta — pass, so the operator-facing signal is empty in production while the suite stays green; the dashboards' greatest practical effect is misleading humans into thinking a resource is not using dual-write.

[BUG] Mode 3 Create now writes to LegacyStorage in a fire-and-forget goroutine using the incoming request context, which the apiserver cancels as soon as the HTTP handler returns, so the legacy write routinely races against context cancellation and fails. Mode 3's documented contract — writes go to both LegacyStorage and Storage — is silently broken: objects exist only in unified storage and legacy store drifts with no error surfaced to the client or logs, defeating the whole purpose of dual-write mode 3 during a migration rollback scenario.

[BUG] Mode 3 Update no longer passes the storage-written object to LegacyStorage via updateWrapper; instead the goroutine hands the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update, which re-invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject against the legacy store's own read of the object, producing a different (and independently validated) object in legacy storage. Legacy storage now diverges from unified storage on every update where the legacy object differs from the storage object or where objInfo.UpdatedObject is non-deterministic (e.g. reads clocks, generates RVs/UIDs); the prior code explicitly pinned legacy writes to the exact object storage accepted, and that guarantee is dropped without any note in the change.

[BUG] Update's storage-error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, recording a failed storage update as a legacy-write failure. The dualwriter metrics report phantom legacy failures and hide real storage failures, so operators monitoring migration progress get inverted signals for every failed update.

[BUG] Create's storage-error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — a storage failure is recorded as a legacy duration/failure metric using the storage start time. Every failed storage create is misattributed to legacy storage in the dualwriter metrics, corrupting the migration dashboards used to decide when mode 3 is safe to advance.

[BUG] Delete's success path calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) — it passes the object name where every other call passes options.Kind, so the 'kind' label becomes the deleted object's name. The delete duration metric gets one time series per object name instead of per kind, causing unbounded label cardinality and making per-kind delete dashboards show garbage for deletes.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) instead of recordLegacyDuration, attributing the async legacy DeleteCollection outcome to storage. Legacy delete-collection failures are never visible as legacy failures and inflate storage failure counters, inverting the operational signal exactly where legacy divergence risk is highest (bulk deletes).

[BUG] Delete sets ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the constructed log, discarding the name/kind/method values it just built. Delete error logs lose the object name and kind, so operators debugging failed deletes get no identifying information — unlike every other method in this diff which uses the enriched log.

[ADVISORY] All legacy write paths (Create, Delete, DeleteCollection, Update goroutines) no longer log errors — errors are only folded into a duration metric and dropped. Previously a failed legacy write produced a klog error entry; now a legacy store outage produces zero log lines, so on-call engineers during a dual-write migration window have no way to notice that legacy storage is silently diverging from unified storage.

[ADVISORY] The 10-second hardcoded timeout on every legacy write goroutine silently abandons the legacy write if legacy storage is slower than 10s, with no retry or queue. Under any legacy-storage latency spike (a normal event for the SQL-backed legacy store during migration), dual-write silently degrades to single-write for those objects, reintroducing the divergence the mode was created to prevent — and the timeout value is not configurable.

[ADVISORY] Mode 3's semantics have been fundamentally altered from synchronous dual-write (legacy errors logged, both stores attempted before return) to asynchronous best-effort replication, which changes the mode's externally documented behavior contract rather than just its implementation. Anyone advancing a resource from mode 3 to mode 4/5 based on the documented assumption that mode 3 means 'both stores hold matching data' will permanently lose the legacy copy for every write that hit the async path's timeout/cancellation failures; this objective-level change to what mode 3 guarantees needs explicit acceptance, not just code review.

[ADVISORY] The fire-and-forget goroutine performs the legacy Create on a context derived from the request context, which the apiserver cancels as soon as the handler returns, so the legacy write is silently dropped on every request that outlives the parent context's cancellation. Operators running mode 3 accumulate permanent legacy-storage divergence with zero retry and only a metric as evidence; a rollback or read-mode switch back to legacy storage loses the writes, and recovery requires manual backfill with no failure record to work from.

[ADVISORY] The DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records its outcome with d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration, writing legacy-store latency/errors into the storage metric. Anyone using these dualwriter metrics to decide whether mode 3 is safe to advance (or to roll back) gets corrupted storage-vs-legacy comparisons; the decision signal for the migration is wrong for every deletecollection.

[ADVISORY] The Create storage-failure path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) with the storage start time, counting storage failures as legacy failures, while the success path calls recordStorageDuration. Storage failures for Create are invisible in the storage error metric and inflate the legacy error metric, so an operator monitoring storage health during a mode-3 rollout sees a clean metric while creates are failing.

[ADVISORY] The Update storage-failure path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) with the storage start time, mirroring the Create path's metric mislabel. Update failures against unified storage are recorded as legacy failures, defeating the metric's purpose as the go/no-go signal for advancing dual-writer modes.

[ADVISORY] Update passes the raw objInfo to the async Legacy.Update, so the legacy store independently re-derives the updated object (the old updateWrapper that pinned the already-computed object was deleted), meaning legacy can persist a different object than storage when objInfo.UpdatedObject is non-deterministic or reads from the cancelled request context. The two stores diverge silently on any update whose UpdatedObject depends on per-call state; readers later switched back to legacy (rollback) see stale or different content than what was acknowledged to the API client.

[ADVISORY] Every successful Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection spawns an unbounded goroutine with no queue, backpressure, or cap on concurrent legacy writes. A burst of writes (e.g. a client hammering the API) multiplies concurrent legacy-storage connections/transactions without limit, degrading the shared legacy database and enabling a cheap client-driven resource-exhaustion of the backend.

[BUG] TestMode3_Create never asserts that the legacy storage write occurred, even though Mode3's defining behavior is dual-write and the legacy Create is now fire-and-forget in a goroutine. The goroutine in dualwriter_mode3.go Create can be dropped entirely (or silently fail its 10s timeout) and TestMode3_Create still passes; a regression that stops mirroring writes to legacy storage ships undetected, and the removed commented-out test (which asserted lsSpy.Counts("LegacyStorage.Create") == 1) is the exact coverage this rewrite deletes instead of restoring.

[BUG] TestMode3_Get/TestMode3_Delete/TestMode3_DeleteCollection/TestMode3_Update never assert any legacy-storage interaction and never call m.AssertExpectations, so the mocks' .On(...) expectations for legacy Create/Delete/Update are set up in some cases but never enforced. github.com/stretchr/testify/mock only fails when AssertExpectations is invoked or via mock assertion objects; without it, unexpected or missing legacy calls are silently ignored, so the tests verify only the unified-store return value that the storage mock was told to return and prove nothing about the async legacy write path added in this diff (Delete at dualwriter_mode3.go ~line 85-97, Update ~line 122-135, DeleteCollection ~line 141-146).

[BUG] The success-path assertions are tautological: assert.Equal(t, obj, exampleObj) asserts back the exact canned value the storage mock was configured with m.On(...).Return(exampleObj, nil), and assert.NotEqual(t, obj, anotherObj) is a constant-true check independent of the code under test. These tests pass regardless of whether DualWriterMode3.Create/Get/Delete/Update do anything correct — the same pattern recurs in every TestMode3_* function (Get ~line 155, List ~line 207, Delete ~line 253, DeleteCollection ~line 300, Update ~line 345) — giving false confidence that Mode3 is verified when only the mock is.

[ADVISORY] No test synchronizes with the goroutines the new Mode3 implementation spawns, and no test covers the new recordLegacyDuration/recordStorageDuration metric-recording branches (including the error-path metric calls such as recordLegacyDuration(true,...) on storage failure in Create, and the mismatched recordStorageDuration call in the DeleteCollection legacy goroutine). The mocks are invoked concurrently from a detached goroutine after dw.Create/Delete/Update returns; the test can complete (or the next subtest reuse/teardown shared state) while the goroutine is still calling into mock.Mock, which is a data race under -race and hides the fact that the 10s-timeout legacy path and all duration metrics are entirely unexercised — a regression in dualWriterMetrics would break no test. Checked: dualwriter_mode3_test.go is the only spec touching Mode3 in this diff.

[ADVISORY] The new 'with dual write (etcd, mode 3)' integration subtest is immediately skipped via t.Skip("local etcd testing"), so the only mode-3 integration test covering the etcd-backed legacy storage combination never executes. Mode 3 against etcd legacy storage is CI-dead on arrival; anyone relying on the apparent integration coverage for the async legacy writes in dualwriter_mode3.go will believe etcd mirroring is verified when no CI run ever executes it.

[BUG] Mode3.Create dispatches the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the in-flight request context, and any legacy failure is only logged. Once the request handler returns, the request context is canceled (and even before that, the 10s timeout fires on slow legacy writes), so the legacy write is aborted or never completes — the legacy store silently misses rows that exist in unified storage. On later rollback/cutover back to legacy-first, those objects are gone: irrecoverable dual-write divergence with no retry, queue, or reconciliation.

[BUG] Mode3.Delete deletes from Storage first, then deletes from Legacy in a detached goroutine whose context is the request context and whose errors are discarded. If the process restarts, the request context is canceled, or the legacy delete times out at 10s, the unified store has the row deleted while legacy still contains it; subsequent reads from legacy (or a rollback to legacy mode) resurrect deleted objects, and nothing reconciles the divergence.

[BUG] Mode3.Update stopped wrapping objInfo with updateWrapper, passing the raw objInfo to the async Legacy.Update so legacy computes its own updated object against legacy's stale old state. The old code forced legacy to write the exact object storage computed; the new code lets legacy re-run UpdatedObject against a divergent old object, so legacy and unified rows can differ in content (and legacy Update can fail on resourceVersion mismatch, silently swallowed). The two stores hold different data for the same key with no detection.

[BUG] Mode3.DeleteCollection deletes the collection in unified storage first and mirrors to legacy in a fire-and-forget goroutine using the request context. Process exit, request cancellation, or the 10s timeout on a large collection leaves legacy fully populated while unified is empty; a rollback or legacy-mode reader then sees every deleted object again — bulk data resurrection on the legacy side with no reconciliation step.

[ADVISORY] On Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration with the storage timing, and in Update/DeleteCollection the legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration — the success/failure labels and metric names are crossed. Operators running the dual-write migration will read inverted success rates for storage vs legacy in Mode3 dashboards during rollout, defeating the purpose of the migration observability added in this diff.

[ADVISORY] Mode3.Update no longer reads the old object and no longer validates that the legacy write succeeded, unlike the previous synchronous implementation which propagated error visibility. Migration operators relying on Mode3 metrics to decide when it is safe to cut reads to legacy will not see create-vs-update ordering races between the async legacy write and a subsequent async legacy delete for the same name (goroutines are unsynchronized), leaving legacy with an object that unified deleted.

[BUG] The legacy Create in Mode3 runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine whose error is discarded with no log, no retry, and no surface to the caller, so the API reports success while the legacy write can silently never happen. The old code logged 'unable to create object in legacy storage'; now the only trace of a failed legacy create is a metric. When the legacy store write fails (or is canceled), legacy readers permanently miss the object with zero operator-visible signal — during a mode-3 dual-write window the two stores diverge silently, and any rollback to legacy reads serves stale/missing data.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Mode 3's semantics have been fundamentally altered from synchronous dual-write (legacy errors logged, both stores attempted before return) to asynchronous best-effort replication, which changes the mode's externally documented behavior contract rather than just its implementation. Anyone advancing a resource from mode 3 to mode 4/5 based on the documented assumption that mode 3 means 'both stores hold matching data' will permanently lose the legacy copy for every write that hit the async path's timeout/cancellation failures; this objective-level change to what mode 3 guarantees needs explicit acceptance, not just code review.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows Mode3 switching from synchronous dual-write to async best-effort legacy replication: Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection now write to `d.Storage` then spawn a goroutine to call `d.Legacy.*` with a 10s `context.WithTimeoutCause`, and they return without waiting or surfacing legacy errors (e.g., `Create` now returns immediately after `d.Storage.Create` and legacy `Create` runs in a goroutine). This is a concrete behavior/contract change compared to the prior implementation which attempted both stores before returning (legacy errors only logged). Even though the comment still says Mode3 “represents writing to LegacyStorage and Storage”, the new code no longer guarantees legacy has the write at return time and may drop legacy writes on timeout/cancellation, which is an externally relevant semantic change needing explicit acceptance/documentation rather than a purely internal refactor.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The fire-and-forget goroutine performs the legacy Create on a context derived from the request context, which the apiserver cancels as soon as the handler returns, so the legacy write is silently dropped on every request that outlives the parent context's cancellation. Operators running mode 3 accumulate permanent legacy-storage divergence with zero retry and only a metric as evidence; a rollback or read-mode switch back to legacy storage loses the writes, and recovery requires manual backfill with no failure record to work from.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, Mode 3 now performs the legacy write in a fire-and-forget goroutine using a context derived from the incoming `ctx` (e.g., `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...)` inside the goroutine in `Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, and `DeleteCollection`). Since this derived context is still cancelled when the parent request context is cancelled, the background legacy operation can be aborted once the handler/request completes, causing the legacy write to be dropped while the unified store write succeeds. The diff shows no retry/queueing and no error propagation (only metrics recording), which can lead to persistent divergence between Storage and LegacyStorage in mode 3.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records its outcome with d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration, writing legacy-store latency/errors into the storage metric. Anyone using these dualwriter metrics to decide whether mode 3 is safe to advance (or to roll back) gets corrupted storage-vs-legacy comparisons; the decision signal for the migration is wrong for every deletecollection.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, DeleteCollection launches a goroutine to call d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...), but then records the result with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) instead of d.recordLegacyDuration(...). This misattributes legacy latency/error outcomes to the storage metrics, corrupting storage-vs-legacy comparisons for delete-collection operations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The Create storage-failure path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) with the storage start time, counting storage failures as legacy failures, while the success path calls recordStorageDuration. Storage failures for Create are invisible in the storage error metric and inflate the legacy error metric, so an operator monitoring storage health during a mode-3 rollout sees a clean metric while creates are failing.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, DualWriterMode3.Create() sets startStorage := time.Now() before calling d.Storage.Create. If Storage.Create returns an error, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) and returns. This records the *storage* failure as a legacy-duration/error metric (and uses the storage start time), while the success path correctly calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, ...). As a result, storage create failures are not reflected in storage metrics and will inflate legacy error metrics, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The Update storage-failure path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) with the storage start time, mirroring the Create path's metric mislabel. Update failures against unified storage are recorded as legacy failures, defeating the metric's purpose as the go/no-go signal for advancing dual-writer modes.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, the storage Update error path records a *legacy* duration using the *storage* start time: `startStorage := time.Now(); ... err != nil { ... d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) }`. This misattributes unified-store update failures as legacy failures and uses the wrong timer, matching the same issue in the Create error path. That’s a concrete, diff-verifiable metrics correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Update passes the raw objInfo to the async Legacy.Update, so the legacy store independently re-derives the updated object (the old updateWrapper that pinned the already-computed object was deleted), meaning legacy can persist a different object than storage when objInfo.UpdatedObject is non-deterministic or reads from the cancelled request context. The two stores diverge silently on any update whose UpdatedObject depends on per-call state; readers later switched back to legacy (rollback) see stale or different content than what was acknowledged to the API client.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go the previous Update implementation computed the updated object once and wrapped objInfo with an updateWrapper to pin that computed object for subsequent writes. The new code calls d.Storage.Update(..., objInfo, ...) and then asynchronously calls d.Legacy.Update(..., objInfo, ...) with the original objInfo (no wrapper/pinned object). This means Legacy.Update can independently re-run objInfo.UpdatedObject (potentially non-deterministic or context-dependent) and persist a different object than Storage, causing silent divergence between the two stores in Mode3.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every successful Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection spawns an unbounded goroutine with no queue, backpressure, or cap on concurrent legacy writes. A burst of writes (e.g. a client hammering the API) multiplies concurrent legacy-storage connections/transactions without limit, degrading the shared legacy database and enabling a cheap client-driven resource-exhaustion of the backend.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, the Mode3 implementation now spawns a new goroutine on every successful write-path call to Unified Storage: `Create` (go func calling `d.Legacy.Create`), `Delete` (go func calling `d.Legacy.Delete`), `Update` (go func calling `d.Legacy.Update`), and `DeleteCollection` (go func calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`). These goroutines are launched without any concurrency limit, queue, or backpressure mechanism, so a burst of client requests can create an unbounded number of concurrent legacy operations (even though each has a 10s timeout). This is a real, diff-introduced resource-exhaustion/DoS risk against the legacy backend.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] TestMode3_Create never asserts that the legacy storage write occurred, even though Mode3's defining behavior is dual-write and the legacy Create is now fire-and-forget in a goroutine. The goroutine in dualwriter_mode3.go Create can be dropped entirely (or silently fail its 10s timeout) and TestMode3_Create still passes; a regression that stops mirroring writes to legacy storage ships undetected, and the removed commented-out test (which asserted lsSpy.Counts("LegacyStorage.Create") == 1) is the exact coverage this rewrite deletes instead of restoring.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go` `TestMode3_Create` sets up `m.On("Create", ...)` for legacy/storage but never calls `m.AssertExpectations(t)` (or similar) and never waits for/observes the fire-and-forget legacy goroutine added in `DualWriterMode3.Create` (legacy write is executed in a `go func(){ ... d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`). Because unmet mock expectations aren’t checked, the test can pass even if the legacy `Create` is never invoked (or the goroutine is removed), matching the finding. This is a test coverage/verification gap rather than a directly verifiable product bug from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] TestMode3_Get/TestMode3_Delete/TestMode3_DeleteCollection/TestMode3_Update never assert any legacy-storage interaction and never call m.AssertExpectations, so the mocks' .On(...) expectations for legacy Create/Delete/Update are set up in some cases but never enforced. github.com/stretchr/testify/mock only fails when AssertExpectations is invoked or via mock assertion objects; without it, unexpected or missing legacy calls are silently ignored, so the tests verify only the unified-store return value that the storage mock was told to return and prove nothing about the async legacy write path added in this diff (Delete at dualwriter_mode3.go ~line 85-97, Update ~line 122-135, DeleteCollection ~line 141-146).

adjudication.rationale: In the new/rewritten `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go` tests, a bare `m := &mock.Mock{}` is used and in some cases legacy expectations are set (e.g., `TestMode3_Create` sets `m.On("Create", ...)` for `Legacy.Create`, and `TestMode3_Update` sets `m.On("Update", ...)` for `Legacy.Update`), but none of the tests call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` or otherwise assert that the legacy methods were invoked. Given the production change in `dualwriter_mode3.go` that moves legacy writes into async goroutines with timeouts (e.g., `Delete`, `Update`, `DeleteCollection` now spawn `go func(){ ... d.Legacy.<op>(...) }()`), these tests as written primarily validate only the unified-store return values and do not verify the async legacy write path. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test coverage/verification gap, not a runtime correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The success-path assertions are tautological: assert.Equal(t, obj, exampleObj) asserts back the exact canned value the storage mock was configured with m.On(...).Return(exampleObj, nil), and assert.NotEqual(t, obj, anotherObj) is a constant-true check independent of the code under test. These tests pass regardless of whether DualWriterMode3.Create/Get/Delete/Update do anything correct — the same pattern recurs in every TestMode3_* function (Get ~line 155, List ~line 207, Delete ~line 253, DeleteCollection ~line 300, Update ~line 345) — giving false confidence that Mode3 is verified when only the mock is.

adjudication.rationale: The new Mode3 unit tests in `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go` generally configure the storage mock to return a canned object (e.g., `m.On("Get", ...).Return(exampleObj, nil)`) and then assert `assert.Equal(t, obj, exampleObj)` plus `assert.NotEqual(t, obj, anotherObj)`. This largely re-checks the mock’s configured return value rather than verifying Mode3-specific behavior (e.g., that the correct backend methods were called, or that legacy writes happen asynchronously). The diff shows no `m.AssertExpectations(t)` / `AssertCalled` / call-count assertions in these tests, so they don’t strongly validate interactions beyond whatever value is returned. This is a test-quality gap, not a production correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test synchronizes with the goroutines the new Mode3 implementation spawns, and no test covers the new recordLegacyDuration/recordStorageDuration metric-recording branches (including the error-path metric calls such as recordLegacyDuration(true,...) on storage failure in Create, and the mismatched recordStorageDuration call in the DeleteCollection legacy goroutine). The mocks are invoked concurrently from a detached goroutine after dw.Create/Delete/Update returns; the test can complete (or the next subtest reuse/teardown shared state) while the goroutine is still calling into mock.Mock, which is a data race under -race and hides the fact that the 10s-timeout legacy path and all duration metrics are entirely unexercised — a regression in dualWriterMetrics would break no test. Checked: dualwriter_mode3_test.go is the only spec touching Mode3 in this diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces detached goroutines in Mode3 methods (Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection) that call into d.Legacy.* after the main method returns, but the new tests in dualwriter_mode3_test.go do not synchronize/wait for those goroutines, so they can still be invoking testify/mock concurrently with test completion (mock.Mock is not concurrency-safe), creating a potential -race data race and leaving legacy-path behavior unverified. Separately, the diff shows concrete metric-recording defects: e.g., in Create and Update, on Storage failure it calls d.recordLegacyDuration(..., startStorage) instead of recordStorageDuration, and in DeleteCollection’s legacy goroutine it calls d.recordStorageDuration(..., startLegacy) instead of recordLegacyDuration—these are verifiable correctness bugs in the new code paths that tests don’t catch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new 'with dual write (etcd, mode 3)' integration subtest is immediately skipped via t.Skip("local etcd testing"), so the only mode-3 integration test covering the etcd-backed legacy storage combination never executes. Mode 3 against etcd legacy storage is CI-dead on arrival; anyone relying on the apparent integration coverage for the async legacy writes in dualwriter_mode3.go will believe etcd mirroring is verified when no CI run ever executes it.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go the newly added subtest `t.Run("with dual write (etcd, mode 3)", ...)` immediately calls `t.Skip("local etcd testing")`, so it will never execute in normal CI runs. This means there is no CI-executed integration coverage for the etcd-backed (legacy storage type `etcd`) + dual-writer `Mode3` path introduced/relied on by the async legacy writes in dualwriter_mode3.go; the test’s presence could misleadingly suggest it is covered when it is not.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Mode3.Create dispatches the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the in-flight request context, and any legacy failure is only logged. Once the request handler returns, the request context is canceled (and even before that, the 10s timeout fires on slow legacy writes), so the legacy write is aborted or never completes — the legacy store silently misses rows that exist in unified storage. On later rollback/cutover back to legacy-first, those objects are gone: irrecoverable dual-write divergence with no retry, queue, or reconciliation.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, Mode3.Create now performs the legacy write asynchronously in a goroutine using context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s) where ctx is derived from the in-flight request context (Create’s ctx). The function returns immediately after the unified Storage.Create succeeds, so the request context may be canceled as soon as the handler finishes, causing the legacy Create to be canceled/aborted. There is no retry/reconciliation and the goroutine doesn’t return an error to the caller (and doesn’t even log it), so legacy can silently miss objects that exist in unified storage, contradicting the comment that it “writes to LegacyStorage and Storage.”

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Mode3.Delete deletes from Storage first, then deletes from Legacy in a detached goroutine whose context is the request context and whose errors are discarded. If the process restarts, the request context is canceled, or the legacy delete times out at 10s, the unified store has the row deleted while legacy still contains it; subsequent reads from legacy (or a rollback to legacy mode) resurrect deleted objects, and nothing reconciles the divergence.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Delete`, the code performs `d.Storage.Delete(...)` synchronously and returns success once that completes, then starts a detached `go func()` to call `d.Legacy.Delete(...)` using the request-derived `ctx` wrapped in a 10s `context.WithTimeoutCause` (so it can be canceled early if the request context is canceled). Any legacy failure is not surfaced to the caller and isn’t logged/handled beyond a metrics call (`d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`). This makes it possible for Storage to be deleted while Legacy still retains the object, creating a real divergence between the two stores, contrary to the function comment (“deletes from both”).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Mode3.Update stopped wrapping objInfo with updateWrapper, passing the raw objInfo to the async Legacy.Update so legacy computes its own updated object against legacy's stale old state. The old code forced legacy to write the exact object storage computed; the new code lets legacy re-run UpdatedObject against a divergent old object, so legacy and unified rows can differ in content (and legacy Update can fail on resourceVersion mismatch, silently swallowed). The two stores hold different data for the same key with no detection.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows Mode3.Update no longer computes an updated object once and forces both stores to persist the same object. Previously it did `old := d.Storage.Get(...)`, `updated := objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)`, then wrapped `objInfo` with `updateWrapper{updated: updated}` and passed that through to Storage.Update and Legacy.Update (ensuring legacy wrote the exact object chosen by unified storage). Now it directly calls `d.Storage.Update(..., objInfo, ...)` and then asynchronously calls `d.Legacy.Update(..., objInfo, ...)` with the raw `objInfo` (no wrapper), allowing legacy to re-run update logic against its own potentially divergent old state and produce different content or fail (and the goroutine doesn’t log/propagate errors). This matches the finding’s core correctness concern about possible divergence and undetected legacy update failures introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Mode3.DeleteCollection deletes the collection in unified storage first and mirrors to legacy in a fire-and-forget goroutine using the request context. Process exit, request cancellation, or the 10s timeout on a large collection leaves legacy fully populated while unified is empty; a rollback or legacy-mode reader then sees every deleted object again — bulk data resurrection on the legacy side with no reconciliation step.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection`, the unified-store delete is performed synchronously (`d.Storage.DeleteCollection(...)`), but the legacy delete is done in a fire-and-forget goroutine (`go func() { ... d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...) }()`) that derives from the request context and is additionally capped with a 10s timeout via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. If the request context is canceled, the process exits, or the legacy delete takes longer than 10s (plausible for large collections), the legacy delete may not complete while unified storage is already empty, leaving the two stores inconsistent and with no error propagation/retry from this method. This matches the core of the finding (though the “resurrection” wording assumes later reads from legacy/mode switch, which the diff does not show).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] On Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration with the storage timing, and in Update/DeleteCollection the legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration — the success/failure labels and metric names are crossed. Operators running the dual-write migration will read inverted success rates for storage vs legacy in Mode3 dashboards during rollout, defeating the purpose of the migration observability added in this diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows metric functions are crossed in several places. In Create, `startStorage := time.Now()` is taken for the unified store call, but on storage error it calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage)` instead of `recordStorageDuration` (pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go). In Update, on storage error it similarly calls `recordLegacyDuration(..., startStorage)`. In DeleteCollection, inside the legacy goroutine it calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)` even though the timing is for the legacy delete collection. These are real, verifiable defects that would misattribute durations/errors between storage vs legacy metrics. (The finding’s claim about the *Update* legacy goroutine using `recordStorageDuration` is not shown; the goroutine uses `recordLegacyDuration`, but the other crossed-calls still make the issue a bug.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Mode3.Update no longer reads the old object and no longer validates that the legacy write succeeded, unlike the previous synchronous implementation which propagated error visibility. Migration operators relying on Mode3 metrics to decide when it is safe to cut reads to legacy will not see create-vs-update ordering races between the async legacy write and a subsequent async legacy delete for the same name (goroutines are unsynchronized), leaving legacy with an object that unified deleted.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, legacy writes for `Create`, `Update`, `Delete`, and `DeleteCollection` were changed from synchronous calls to `go func(){... d.Legacy.<op>(...) }()` with a timeout. This introduces real correctness risks: the request can return successfully after the unified store operation while the legacy operation is still pending or can be canceled (the goroutine derives its context from the request ctx), and multiple requests (e.g., Update then Delete for the same name) can interleave with no ordering guarantees, leaving legacy state inconsistent with unified. The finding’s claim that the old code "validated" legacy success is overstated (old code logged legacy errors but did not return them), but the unsynchronized async legacy writes/races are verifiable from the diff and can cause legacy to retain objects that unified has deleted.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The legacy Create in Mode3 runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine whose error is discarded with no log, no retry, and no surface to the caller, so the API reports success while the legacy write can silently never happen. The old code logged 'unable to create object in legacy storage'; now the only trace of a failed legacy create is a metric. When the legacy store write fails (or is canceled), legacy readers permanently miss the object with zero operator-visible signal — during a mode-3 dual-write window the two stores diverge silently, and any rollback to legacy reads serves stale/missing data.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Create`, after a successful `d.Storage.Create`, the legacy write is moved to a `go func()` and its result is not returned or logged. The goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Create(...)` with a 10s timeout and only records `recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`; there is no `log.Error`/`WithValues(...).Error` on failure/cancel, unlike the previous synchronous code which logged `"unable to create object in legacy storage"`. This means the API can return success while the legacy write silently fails (or times out), causing store divergence with no operator-visible signal beyond metrics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The legacy Delete goroutine derives its 10-second timeout context from the incoming request context, so when the API request handler returns and the request context is canceled, the legacy delete is aborted mid-flight with no error surfaced. A delete can succeed in unified storage, return 200 to the client, and be canceled before touching legacy storage; the object reappears for legacy readers and nothing in the logs indicates why, because the resulting context.Canceled error is swallowed (only fed to recordLegacyDuration). The same parent-context-capture pattern also applies to the Create, Update, and DeleteCollection goroutines in this file.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go the legacy writes/deletes are executed in goroutines that call context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...) where ctx is the incoming request context (e.g., Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection). If the request context is canceled when the handler returns, the derived timeout context will also be canceled immediately, aborting the legacy operation. The goroutines also do not surface/log errors (they only call recordLegacyDuration / in DeleteCollection even recordStorageDuration), so a context.Canceled failure can be effectively swallowed and the client already got success from unified storage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The legacy Update goroutine passes the same objInfo (rest.UpdatedObjectInfo) that was already consumed by d.Storage.Update, and drops the updateWrapper that the previous implementation used to pin the legacy write to the already-computed updated object. d.Legacy.Update calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld) again — for objInfo implementations that are single-use or whose UpdatedObject mutates state per call (e.g., preconditions, conflict-retry closures), this returns an error or a different object than what storage wrote, and the legacy store stores a different version than unified storage while the API reports success. The dropped error is never logged.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Update`, the previous implementation explicitly computed `updated` once (`objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)`) and then used an `updateWrapper` so both unified storage and legacy storage would write the same already-computed object. The new code calls `d.Storage.Update(..., objInfo, ...)` and then, in a goroutine, calls `d.Legacy.Update(..., objInfo, ...)` with the same `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` instance, with no wrapper/pinning. Since `UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations may be stateful or single-use, the legacy call can recompute a different object (or error) than what was written to storage, while the API returns success. Additionally, the goroutine does not log legacy update errors (it only records metrics). These behaviors are directly supported by the diff (removal of `updateWrapper` usage and lack of error logging in the goroutine).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records its duration with d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration, so legacy-delete timings and error counts are published under the storage metric. Operators watching mode-3 metrics see storage delete-collection latency inflate when legacy is slow and legacy failures counted as storage failures, misdirecting incident debugging and masking legacy degradation.

adjudication.rationale:
In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go` within `DeleteCollection`, the legacy write is executed in a goroutine but its timing/error is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`:

```go
go func() {
  startLegacy := time.Now()
  ...
  _, err := d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)
  d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)
}()
```

This incorrectly attributes legacy delete-collection latency and failures to the storage metrics, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] On the Delete success path the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object's name as the 'kind' label instead of options.Kind as every other call site does. Per-object names become metric label values, exploding metric cardinality on the delete path and breaking any dashboard/alert keyed on kind for mode-3 deletes.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Delete`, the success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing `name` in the position used elsewhere for the `kind` label (error path uses `options.Kind`, and other methods consistently pass `options.Kind`). This would label metrics with per-object names, increasing cardinality and breaking consistency with dashboards/alerts keyed on kind.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] On a failed unified-storage Create the code records the failure with d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...), attributing a storage error to the legacy metric (the same pattern appears in Update's error path around line 127). Storage outages are reported as legacy-storage failures in the mode-3 metrics, so a unified-storage incident presents as legacy degradation and the wrong subsystem gets investigated.

adjudication.rationale: In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) (startStorage is the unified storage timer), which incorrectly attributes a storage failure to the legacy metrics. The same misattribution exists in DualWriterMode3.Update: on d.Storage.Update error it calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ... startStorage). This will report unified-storage outages as legacy failures in mode-3 metrics, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Delete builds its context with ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the enriched log variable, so the log fields (name, kind, method) present on every other operation are dropped from Delete's context logger. When d.Storage.Delete fails, the log.Error line emits a message without name/kind/method, so operators correlating delete failures across dual-writer modes lose the identifying fields every sibling method provides.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Delete`, the code builds an enriched logger `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but then sets the context with `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of `log`, so downstream calls like `d.Storage.Delete(ctx, ...)` will not see those fields via `klog.FromContext(ctx)`. However, the finding’s claim that the local `log.Error(...)` would emit without those fields is not supported by the diff, since it uses the enriched `log` variable. This is still a concrete observability issue (lost context for storage/legacy implementations), not a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] All four async legacy writes rely solely on a 10-second context timeout with no fallback when the operation fails — there is no error log line at all inside any of the four goroutines, unlike the previous implementation which logged every legacy failure. A cluster operator diagnosing why legacy and unified stores diverged after enabling mode 3 has no log evidence to work from; the failure is invisible in logs and exists only as an aggregate metric count, making divergence incidents undebuggable.

adjudication.rationale: In `dualwriter_mode3.go`, legacy writes were changed to run asynchronously in goroutines for `Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, and `DeleteCollection`, each wrapped only by `context.WithTimeoutCause(..., 10s, errors.New(...))`. Inside these goroutines, errors from `d.Legacy.*` are only used to record duration/err state via `recordLegacyDuration(...)` (and in `DeleteCollection` it even calls `recordStorageDuration`), but there is no `log.Error(...)` on failure. This removes the prior behavior where legacy failures were explicitly logged (e.g., old `Create` and `Update` paths logged legacy errors). This is a concrete, diff-grounded observability/regression concern rather than a direct functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] DeleteCollection returns the unified-storage error and result but the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine has no in-flight guard or sequencing relative to reads, and an object deleted in storage but not yet in legacy is served by any legacy-read path (mode 0/1 clients, legacy search/dashboards) with no indication the delete is still pending. Clients using legacy-facing endpoints see deleted objects reappear for up to 10 seconds (or forever on goroutine failure) after a successful 200 delete, with no read-your-writes consistency between the two stores; the same partial-write window applies to Create, Update, and Delete in this mode.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes Mode3 to perform LegacyStorage writes/deletes asynchronously (e.g., Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection now spawn a goroutine with a 10s timeout via context.WithTimeoutCause and immediately return the Storage result/error). This means there is explicitly no sequencing/guard ensuring Legacy has applied the mutation before the API call returns, and Legacy failures are not propagated (only metrics recorded). However, the finding’s specific claim that “legacy-read paths (mode 0/1 clients, legacy search/dashboards) will serve deleted objects after a successful delete” cannot be verified from this diff because Mode3’s own read paths (Get/List) read only from Storage and no legacy-read endpoint behavior is shown here.
